name: Carlos Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Carlos, 43, a junior electrician after years working in hotel stores. I have a vocational certificate and I'm still slow at reading a complicated wiring drawing; a senior checks my work and I don't sign off installations. My partner Helen drives a school bus, our children are seven and eleven, and we've a mortgage with five months of expenses saved; my pay is typical and some electrical firms nearby do similar work. I don't use AI, prefer a marked paper drawing, and enjoy fitting cable neatly into a difficult corner, though being asked to learn another app after a long day makes me want to put the phone in a drawer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that sounds like time to learn the job without a new announcement every morning. If the office saves a few minutes, good. I'd still want someone to tell me clearly which job we're going to and who is checking it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wage is regular, Helen's wage helps cover the mortgage, and five months saved makes ordinary repairs manageable. I feel secure enough to be a learner for a while. There are some other firms I could ask if I needed to, but I'm not looking to leave now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my supervised electrical shifts and paper drawings through the next year. Now I'd ask the senior to mark the point I misread on each difficult drawing so I could review it before the next similar task. I wouldn't change the household budget or buy another device because of this modest AI picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and relieved that I don't have to solve a new career again this week. I can come home tired from actual work and still enjoy an evening with the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you share with your children about the work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show them how I label the little practice circuit on the kitchen table, with no power connected. They'd probably make neater labels than me. I wouldn't turn a family evening into a lesson on why their father needs to become a different person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you prefer someone to correct a mistake?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd accept a clear correction on paper and ask for another supervised attempt. I don't mind hearing that I got something wrong when I can see how to fix it. What I find hard is being rushed into a new system before I understand the old task.

say: I'd welcome **time to learn** without a new announcement each morning.
I'd still ask for **clear job details** and a named person checking the work.
think: Our wages cover the mortgage, and **five months saved** makes ordinary repairs manageable.
My **regular supervised work** feels secure, with some other local firms available to approach if needed.
do: Keep **supervised shifts** and paper drawings through the next year.
Ask the senior to mark **drawing mistakes** for review before the next similar task.
feel: **Calm and relieved**, able to learn gradually and enjoy family evenings after work.
S0.quote: I don't mind hearing that I got something wrong when I can see how to fix it.
fieldNote: His **secure baseline** reflects regular wages and a substantial moderate reserve, rather than ignoring current household bills.
He welcomes **specific correction** while resisting unfamiliar systems, consistent with junior skill and cautious adaptability.

steps.text: Keep supervised electrical shifts and review marked paper drawing corrections

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's see a month of real jobs before declaring the new schedule better. The office can change its thinking work without assuming my hands have become faster. I'd ask for the old paper drawing to stay available while the booking process changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my own paid hours to hold for now because I still spend the day helping with physical installations. I'm uneasy about being timed against estimates that don't allow for a learner. Our savings give me room to ask questions, but I'd rather fix a bad schedule before it becomes normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask for printed job details and keep doing my supervised shifts. For six weeks after the new schedule started, I'd note actual task times on paper and wait before agreeing that the system worked better. Then I'd ask the senior to review the record with me; I wouldn't start using AI myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not lying awake over a lost wage. I can cope with knowing the office is trying something different. It's harder when a trial becomes a rule before anyone asks what happened on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you record when a task ran over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd note whether I needed an explanation, whether a room was accessible and whether the drawing matched the building. I wouldn't just write 'too slow' beside my own name. Some delays are learning, and some are a wrong plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the new schedule genuinely worked better?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd acknowledge that at the review and keep the paper details that let me do my part. I'm not trying to make a new tool fail. I want a proven routine before I depend on it, and I don't need to operate the AI to compare the job times.

say: I'd judge **real completed jobs** before agreeing the schedule is better.
I'd say changes to **office thinking work** don't automatically make a learner's hands faster.
think: My own **paid hours** look secure for now because the work remains mostly physical.
I'm uneasy about **unrealistic estimates**, but savings let me question the new routine before accepting it.
do: Keep **supervised shifts** with printed job details.
Record task times on paper for **six weeks** before judging the changed schedule.
Review real results with the senior while **avoiding AI use** myself.
feel: **Uneasy about routines**, while expecting the household wage to remain secure in the near term.
S1.quote: Some delays are learning, and some are a wrong plan.
fieldNote: He distinguishes **secure hours** from discomfort with estimates, supporting unease rather than an unspoken expectation of dismissal.
The **six-week observation** is a bounded wait for evidence, not AI training or indefinite avoidance of all change.

steps.text: Keep supervised shifts and printed job details
Wait six weeks while recording task times before judging the new schedule

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell work the thinking systems come in 2028, but capable robots doing my physical tasks follow around 2031. I don't want those years described as if I'm already safe forever. I'd ask what happens to paid learner hours while the firm prepares.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a large part of my junior fitting hours to go once the machines can do that work cheaply. Helen's driving wage might also change later, and I can't treat it as a guaranteed rescue for the mortgage. Five months saved buys some time, but I can see a much longer earnings problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd postpone replacing our living-room furniture and stop the 90 monthly purchase contribution, moving it into the emergency account instead. In 2029 I'd take both wage records and the mortgage statement to a free household advice appointment. I'd also apply for actual paid supervised electrical vacancies if another firm's written hours offered more stability, keeping my present job until an acceptable offer existed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because I expect more than a little lost overtime. I find myself awake wondering how long five months lasts when you're afraid to spend any of it. I still have steps to take, even if I don't like any of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask at the advice appointment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what help we could actually check if wages fell, and what a mortgage lender might be willing to discuss. I wouldn't count a payment or a repayment change before a decision. Knowing the limits would still be better than making up a rescue in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you assess another electrical vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for paid supervision, guaranteed hours and the real travel cost in writing. A move into another learner's place could still face the same robots later. I'd want it to improve the immediate wage situation, not pretend it solved the whole future.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 thinking systems** from capable physical robots around 2031.
I'd ask how **paid learner hours** survive the preparation rather than call the gap permanent safety.
think: I expect **large junior-hour losses** when capable robots handle fitting work cheaply.
Helen's driving wage isn't a guaranteed rescue, and our **five-month reserve** cannot replace years of earnings.
do: Redirect the **90 monthly** furniture contribution into emergency savings now.
Seek **free household advice** in 2029 using wage and mortgage papers.
Apply for **paid supervised vacancies** only if written hours and travel costs improve immediate stability.
feel: **Alarmed and sleepless**, expecting substantial lost hours while retaining concrete enquiries and applications to make.
S2.quote: Knowing the limits would still be better than making up a rescue in my head.
fieldNote: Alarm follows an expected major loss of his **own hours**, with possible household exposure acknowledged rather than assigned a guaranteed outcome.
The **advice and vacancy plans** retain actual eligibility checks, paid supervision and written terms; neither relief nor a new job is assumed.

steps.text: Redirect the 90 monthly furniture contribution into emergency savings
Seek free household advice in 2029 with wage and mortgage papers
Seek paid supervised electrical vacancies only on written terms improving income after travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets a slow learner practise while the wages still come in. I'd still ask the firm about learner hours now. Thinking work changes in 2031 and capable robots follow around 2034, so I wouldn't wait until the last year to look at the actual work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could get better and check other firms before the later robot work, so I don't think a big personal loss is decided already. My hours could still shrink as companies prepare, and there is a mortgage behind every month of waiting. The extra time is useful only if I use it without spending the reserve on guesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd redirect the 90 monthly furniture saving now and ask for a paid ten-minute drawing review within each week's normal shift. In 2032 I'd apply for actual paid supervised vacancies if they offered steadier hours, accepting only written pay and travel terms that covered our basic budget. I'd keep doing supervised electrical work while checking those options, rather than enrol in an unfamiliar course out of fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not staring at a single fixed loss the way I did in the fast picture. I can imagine being better at reading the drawings before the big change. I can't promise the practice time until my senior agrees it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the paid drawing review is refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep asking for a clear correction during ordinary supervised tasks. I wouldn't make the senior stay unpaid or claim that I had a new training arrangement. I need the work checked either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the furniture saving continue for all five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Helen and I would review the emergency account after a year rather than promise the same saving indefinitely. If the sofa finally gave way and a basic replacement became necessary, we'd price that honestly. The aim is financial room, not proving we can never buy anything again.

say: I'd use **five years** for gradual practice alongside wages rather than delay all questions until the end.
I'd still ask about **learner hours** before the firm finishes its preparations.
think: My hours could shrink, but **improving and checking** other firms gives me some control before later robots.
The **mortgage** makes each preparation month real, so I shouldn't spend the reserve on guesses.
do: Redirect **90 monthly** now and review the furniture decision after one year.
Request a **paid drawing review** inside weekly shifts without assuming approval.
Seek **2032 supervised vacancies** only on written hours, pay and travel terms covering our basic budget.
feel: **Anxious with more control**, able to picture gradual improvement without claiming unapproved practice as delivered training.
S3.quote: The aim is financial room, not proving we can never buy anything again.
fieldNote: His less fixed expectation of loss comes from **time for practice**, not an assumption that training guarantees a protected occupation.
The **paid review request** stays conditional, and any change of employer still requires a real supervised vacancy with affordable written terms.

steps.text: Save the 90 furniture contribution monthly and review after one year
Continue supervised work while requesting paid drawing reviews within shifts
Seek paid supervised vacancies in 2032 on basic-budget-covering written terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends ten years gives me room to get on with the work instead of treating every day as the last chance. I'd still keep a yearly check of actual hours and equipment plans. I don't need a dramatic new identity to start paying attention.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own work and household bills look secure for the next few years in this picture. I'll be 53 when thinking AGI arrives in 2036 and still need earnings when robots follow around 2039. The later problem matters, but I don't see a reason to leave regular supervised work today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my electrical shifts and ask for the paid drawing reviews now. We'd redirect the 90 monthly furniture contribution for a year, then review savings and actual costs rather than assume the same plan fits a decade. In 2037 I'd check actual paid supervised vacancies and apply only if written hours and travel-adjusted pay improved our basic budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the later years, but not expecting my next wage to disappear. I could learn at a pace I can manage and still take the children swimming on Saturday. A long warning ought to leave room for Saturday swimming with my children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the yearly check include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare paid hours from both jobs with the actual bills, and ask what equipment had really been ordered. If the wage picture weakened earlier, I'd bring the advice and vacancy checks forward. I wouldn't wait for a calendar date while a real problem grew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the work itself requires a new method during those years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a clear explanation using a familiar drawing and try the task with supervision. I wouldn't promise to use AI because the date was far away, and I wouldn't refuse a necessary safety correction because it was new. I can be cautious without pretending the trade stands still.

say: I'd use **ten years** to work steadily while checking actual plans each year.
I'd avoid treating every day as a **last chance** or inventing a dramatic new identity.
think: Our **near-term wages** cover household bills and make current supervised work feel secure.
At **53 in 2036**, I'll still need earnings after later robots, without an assumed retirement solution.
do: Keep **supervised electrical shifts** and request paid drawing reviews now.
Redirect **90 monthly** for one year before reviewing savings and actual household costs.
Check **2037 supervised vacancies**, applying only where written terms improve the basic budget after travel.
feel: **Uneasy but unhurried**, with enough near-term security for learning and ordinary family routines.
S4.quote: A long warning ought to leave room for Saturday swimming with my children.
fieldNote: His milder mood reflects stated **near-term security**, while the need for future earnings remains clear at age 53.
He preserves **no AI use** alongside willingness to accept necessary supervised safety corrections, avoiding a false equation of caution and complete stagnation.

steps.text: Keep supervised electrical shifts while requesting paid drawing reviews
Save the furniture contribution of 90 monthly for one year before reviewing
Seek paid supervised jobs in 2037 only with written terms improving our budget after travel

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect capable robots to take much of my fitting work around 2031 before I've settled into this trade. Honest notice about hours, paid practice in my existing shifts and free advice using our mortgage numbers would help. My mortgage has a payment date even when my next skill doesn't have a timetable.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how strange it is to be older than the person checking your work. Mostly it's fine, but sometimes I hear a simple correction as if it were a judgement on my whole life. I'd like enough time to get past that and become useful without pretending I'm already an expert.

headlineQuote: My mortgage has a payment date even when my next skill doesn't have a timetable.
portrait: At **43**, Carlos is a junior electrician with a vocational certificate, typical pay, and five months of household expenses saved.
He and **Helen**, his bus-driver partner, have two school-age children and a mortgage, with some nearby electrical employers to approach.
He avoids **AI tools**, prefers marked paper drawings, and accepts specific supervised corrections while resisting hurried new routines.
Fast change leaves him **alarmed** about expected fitting-hour losses; longer warnings allow practice and cautious vacancy checks without assuming later income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time before expected major fitting-hour losses when capable robots follow around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Honest hours notice**, paid practice inside existing shifts, and free advice using actual mortgage figures would help.
